questions.q: Training ages run from 20 to 60. With min-max normalisation, what does age 35 become?
questions.why: (x − min) / (max − min) = (35 − 20) / (60 − 20) = 15 / 40 = **0.375**. 0.583 divides by the maximum (35 / 60) instead of the range; 1.75 divides by the minimum (35 / 20).

questions.q: You have fitted `StandardScaler` on the training set. How should you scale the test set?
options: Fit a new scaler on the test set and transform it
Leave the test set unscaled
Call `scaler.transform(X_test)`, which applies the training means and standard deviations
Fit the scaler again on training and test together
questions.why: The test set stands in for future data, so it must be transformed with the statistics learned from training only. Refitting on test data (or on everything) lets test information leak in and also puts the two sets on slightly different scales.

questions.q: A training column holds 2, 4, 6 and 8. `StandardScaler` divides by n, not n − 1. What z-score does it give a new value of 10?
options: About 1.94
About 2.24
questions.why: Mean = 5; SD = √((9 + 1 + 1 + 9) / 4) = √5 ≈ 2.236; z = (10 − 5) / 2.236 ≈ **2.24**. Using the n − 1 formula gives SD ≈ 2.582 and z ≈ 1.94, which is what pandas' `.std()` would produce, not StandardScaler.

questions.q: An income column is strongly right-skewed. After standardisation, what does its distribution look like?
options: Normal (bell-shaped), because z-scores are normal
Symmetric around the median
Uniform between −1 and 1
Still right-skewed; only the centre and units change, to mean 0 and SD 1
questions.why: Standardisation shifts and stretches the axis but does not change the shape of the distribution. Believing that z-scoring makes data normal is a common misconception; use a log transform if you need to reduce skew.

questions.q: A min-max scaler fitted on training incomes from ₹5 lakh to ₹50 lakh gives a test customer earning ₹65 lakh a value of 1.33. What does this mean?
options: A bug: min-max values must lie between 0 and 1
The scaler should be refitted on the test set
Nothing is wrong: the customer earns more than anyone in training, so the value lies above 1
The customer should be removed from the test set
questions.why: (65 − 5) / 45 ≈ 1.33. The 0 to 1 range is guaranteed only for the training data; new data can fall outside it, just as a standardised value can exceed the training range. Refitting on test data to "fix" it would cause leakage.

questions.q: Six incomes (₹ lakh): 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 100. With NumPy's default quartiles the median is 9, Q1 = 6.5 and Q3 = 11.5. What does robust scaling turn 12 into?
questions.why: Robust scaling uses (x − median) / IQR = (12 − 9) / (11.5 − 6.5) = 3 / 5 = **0.6**, and 100 becomes 18.2, clearly apart. Min-max would give (12 − 4) / 96 ≈ 0.08, cramming the ordinary customers near 0 because one extreme sets the range.

questions.q: Customer A is (age 30, income ₹5,00,000). B is (31, ₹5,30,000) and C is (55, ₹5,00,000). Unscaled k-NN says C is A's nearest neighbour. How should you read this?
options: Income in rupees dominates the distance (30,000 versus 25), so age is effectively ignored; after standardising, B (one year and ₹30,000 apart) becomes the nearer neighbour
C really is the most similar, because their incomes match exactly
k-NN cannot handle two features
Age should be removed because it disagrees with income
questions.why: Unscaled, A–B ≈ 30,000 and A–C = 25, so a 25-year age gap counts for less than a ₹30,000 income gap. With SDs of, say, 12 years and ₹3 lakh, A–B ≈ 0.13 and A–C ≈ 2.08. Trusting the raw ranking is the trap; scaling can reverse who your neighbours are.

questions.q: Interview: "Why does ridge regression need scaled features when plain linear regression does not?" Which answer is best?
options: Ridge cannot handle negative numbers
Ridge's penalty treats all weights equally, but a weight's size depends on its feature's units; without scaling, features in small units are penalised more harshly than those in large units
Ridge uses distances between rows, like k-NN
Scaling makes ridge regression run without a penalty
questions.why: Plain linear regression just rescales a weight when units change, so predictions are unaffected. Ridge adds a penalty on the size of the weights, and the same effect needs a big weight for income in lakhs but a tiny one for income in rupees. Ridge is not distance-based; that is the tempting confusion with k-NN and SVM.
